subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house opens onto a narrow court, and the weather that day is foggy and bitterly cold.
quote: although the court was of the narrowest, the houses opposite were mere phantoms
why: Fog and cold are weather of the moment; the narrow court is mere setting description, though a later scene could echo it.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house has neighbouring offices across the court whose windows show candles lit.
quote: candles were flaring in the windows of the neighbouring offices
why: Candles in neighbouring windows are set dressing and sensory texture.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Cratchit applauded Fred's speech involuntarily and was immediately sensible of the impropriety.
quote: The clerk in the Tank involuntarily applauded.
why: An in-the-moment reaction, the involuntary applause and his sense of impropriety; nothing lasting depends on it.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge overheard Fred's cordial seasonal greetings to Cratchit at the outer door, and Cratchit returned them warmly.
quote: muttered Scrooge; who overheard him
why: Scrooge overhearing the greeting is a momentary detail; the cordial exchange is a one-off with no lasting dependence.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: Labourers are repairing the gas-pipes in the main street at the corner of the court, and have lit a great fire in a brazier around which ragged men and boys gather.
quote: In the main street, at the corner of the court, some labourers were repairing the gas-pipes, and had lighted a great fire in a brazier
why: Gas-pipe repair and the brazier crowd are transient street texture of the moment.

statement: The fog and darkness thicken and the cold intensifies as Christmas Eve afternoon goes on, after the charity collectors have left.
quote: Meanwhile the fog and darkness thickened so
why: Thickening fog and cold are weather of the moment. The sequence after the collectors left is already covered by events.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge regards giving the clerk Christmas Day off as picking his pocket on the twenty-fifth of December.
quote: A poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December!
why: Scrooge's figurative complaint and opinion in the moment; the narrator's characterization, not a concrete fact to contradict.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Cratchit snuffed out his candle and put on his hat when Scrooge signalled closing time, ending his candle-warmth in the Tank for the day.
quote: who instantly snuffed his candle out, and put on his hat
why: A momentary action at closing time, with nothing later depending on it.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: There is a slide on Cornhill, and boys line up to slide on it on Christmas Eve.
quote: went down a slide on Cornhill, at the end of a lane of boys, twenty times, in honour of its being Christmas Eve
why: Incidental street texture; the slide is a one-off detail the story doesn't return to.

subject: scrooges-counting-house
statement: The counting-house was closed up very quickly once Scrooge left.
quote: The office was closed in a twinkling
why: The quick closing is incidental detail of the moment.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The house has a black old gateway, around which fog and frost hang thickly on this night.
quote: The fog and frost so hung about the black old gateway of the house
why: Fog and frost around the gateway is momentary weather and atmosphere; the black old gateway itself is mere set dressing.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge dismisses the apparition of Marley's face with the word 'Humbug!' and walks across the room.
quote: "Humbug!" said Scrooge; and walked across the room.
why: A momentary dismissive exclamation and walking across the room is a gesture and reaction in the moment that nothing later depends on.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge says he does not believe in the ghost, declaring it humbug, even as it approaches his door.
quote: "It's humbug still!" said Scrooge. "I won't believe it."
why: Scrooge's disbelief in the moment is a reaction; it is superseded by the ghost's presence and is not a fixed fact.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost sits on the opposite side of the fireplace from Scrooge.
quote: the ghost sat down on the opposite side of the fireplace, as if he were quite used to it.
why: Seating position in the moment; incidental staging.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: The ghost's lower jaw drops down upon its breast when it removes the bandage from its head.
quote: the phantom taking off the bandage round its head, as if it were too warm to wear indoors, its lower jaw dropped down upon its breast!
why: A one-off momentary gesture and effect, not depended on later.

subject: jacob-marley
statement: Marley's ghost rebinds its head wrapper afterward, the jaws knocking its teeth together, and ends standing erect with its chain wound over and about its arm.
quote: the spectre took its wrapper from the table, and bound it round its head, as before.
why: Momentary action and posture at scene's end; incidental staging.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge has a toothpick in this scene, which he threatens to swallow as a test.
quote: You see this toothpick?" said Scrooge
why: A momentary prop used in a single exchange; nothing later depends on it.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: After the phantoms and their voices faded, the night became as it had been when Scrooge walked home, and Scrooge then closed the window.
quote: But they and their spirit voices faded together; and the night became as it had been when he walked home.
why: The sequence of the fading and the night returning to normal is a momentary description. Nothing later depends on it.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: A neighbouring church's chimes strike the four quarters and then the hour, and the bell tolled twelve when Scrooge woke.
quote: the chimes of a neighbouring church struck the four quarters
why: Church chime pattern and the twelve strokes in the moment are momentary texture; the bell does return, but this particular chiming is incidental.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The temperature is well below freezing and frost covers the window of Scrooge's bedroom chamber.
quote: the thermometer a long way below freezing
why: Weather and frost of the moment are set dressing in the bedroom.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge holds a financial instrument: a bill of exchange payable 'three days after sight' to Mr. Ebenezer Scrooge or his order.
quote: "three days after sight of this First of Exchange pay to Mr. Ebenezer Scrooge or his order,"
why: The bill of exchange is a hypothetical figure of speech, not a real possession.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: The school's stables hold fowls, and its coach-houses and sheds are overgrown with grass.
quote: Fowls clucked and strutted in the stables; and the coach-houses and sheds were over-run with grass.
why: Set dressing of fowls and grass-grown sheds, unlikely to be revisited.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: The school's interior is poorly furnished, cold and vast, and its atmosphere recalls too much getting up by candle-light and too little to eat.
quote: they found them poorly furnished, cold, and vast.
why: Sensory texture and atmosphere of the interior, not returned to.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: A long, bare schoolroom with plain deal forms and desks lies through a door at the back of the house, across the hall.
quote: a door at the back of the house. It opened before them, and disclosed a long, bare, melancholy room, made barer still by lines of plain deal forms and desks.
why: Layout and furniture of a room seen once; incidental dressing.

subject: boyhood-boarding-school
statement: The school's grounds include a dull yard behind with a half-thawed water-spout and a lone despondent poplar with leafless boughs, plus a store-house with a swinging door.
quote: not a drip from the half-thawed water-spout in the dull yard behind, not a sigh among the leafless boughs of one despondent poplar, not the idle swinging of an empty store-house door
why: Yard details like water-spout, poplar and store-house door are sensory texture in the moment.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge pities his former self, calling him 'Poor boy!'
quote: he said, in pity for his former self, "Poor boy!" and cried again.
why: A momentary feeling of pity and exclamation in the moment.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge dries his eyes with his cuff and puts his hand in his pocket, wishing to give something.
quote: putting his hand in his pocket, and looking about him, after drying his eyes with his cuff
why: A momentary gesture of drying eyes and reaching into his pocket; the wish to give is captured by fact 12.

subject: belle
statement: Belle is a fair young girl who wears a mourning-dress when Scrooge is with her in this scene.
quote: sat by the side of a fair young girl in a mourning-dress
why: The mourning-dress is incidental clothing in a single moment of the vision, though it might hint at a bereavement.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-past
statement: The Ghost's face in this moment shows fragments of all the faces it has shown Scrooge.
quote: a face, in which in some strange way there were fragments of all the faces it had shown him
why: The look of the Ghost's face in this moment is a momentary appearance that nothing later depends on.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge intends to challenge the Spirit the moment it appears and does not want to be taken by surprise.
quote: he wished to challenge the Spirit on the moment of its appearance, and did not wish to be taken by surprise
why: A momentary intention/feeling in the scene; superseded immediately by events and not something later depends on.

subject: scrooges-bedroom
statement: When the clock struck One, a blaze of ruddy light streamed onto Scrooge's bed, with Scrooge at its centre.
quote: he lay upon his bed, the very core and centre of a blaze of ruddy light, which streamed upon it when the clock proclaimed the hour
why: Sensory light description at the moment; the light's source is later explained, but the specific streaming onto the bed is set dressing.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: Scrooge's room is hung with living green: holly, mistletoe and ivy cover the walls and ceiling, with bright berries among them.
quote: The walls and ceiling were so hung with living green, that it looked a perfect grove; from every part of which, bright gleaming berries glistened.
why: Room decoration is set dressing for this scene; the room is transformed and may revert, and later scenes need not recall it.

subject: scrooges-chambers
statement: The hearth in Scrooge's room had never known such a blaze in Scrooge's time, Marley's time, or for many winters before.
quote: such a mighty blaze went roaring up the chimney, as that dull petrification of a hearth had never known in Scrooge's time, or Marley's, or for many and many a winter season gone.
why: A comparative aside about the hearth's blaze; sensory texture of the moment.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-present
statement: The Ghost of Christmas Present sits on a throne-like heap of food on Scrooge's floor: turkeys, geese, game, poultry, brawn, joints of meat, sucking-pigs, sausages, mince-pies, plum-puddings, oysters, chestnuts, apples, oranges, pears, twelfth-cakes and bowls of punch.
quote: Heaped up on the floor, to form a kind of throne, were turkeys, geese, game, poultry, brawn, great joints of meat, sucking-pigs, long wreaths of sausages, mince-pies, plum-puddings, barrels of oysters, red-hot chestnuts, cherry-cheeked apples, juicy oranges, luscious pears, immense twelfth-cakes, and seething bowls of punch
why: The food throne is scene dressing; the feast is not carried forward as a lasting state.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge enters the Spirit's presence timidly and with his head hung, no longer the dogged Scrooge he had been, and does not like to meet the Spirit's eyes.
quote: He was not the dogged Scrooge he had been; and though the Spirit's eyes were clear and kind, he did not like to meet them.
why: A momentary demeanor and reaction (timidity, not meeting eyes) in this scene.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: On Christmas morning the townspeople scrape snow from the pavements in front of their dwellings and from their housetops, and the poulterers' shops are still half open.
quote: The poulterers' shops were still half open
why: Snow-scraping and half-open shops are moment-specific street texture the story is unlikely to return to.

subject: london-city-streets-christmas
statement: On Christmas morning the Grocers' shops are nearly closed, with perhaps one or two shutters down, while customers crowd in.
quote: nearly closed, with perhaps two shutters down, or one
why: The state of the grocers' shutters is set dressing for this one morning.

subject: peter-cratchit
statement: Peter wears a monstrous shirt collar that is Bob's private property, lent for Christmas Day.
quote: the corners of his monstrous shirt collar (Bob's private property, conferred upon his son and heir in honour of the day)
why: The borrowed collar is a one-day detail of Christmas dress and not likely to matter later.

subject: martha-cratchit
statement: Martha saw a countess and a lord some days before, and says the lord was about as tall as Peter.
quote: how she had seen a countess and a lord some days before, and how the lord "was much about as tall as Peter;"
why: A passing anecdote about seeing a lord is chatter with no later dependence.

subject: tiny-tim
statement: Tiny Tim has a plaintive little voice and sang a song about a lost child travelling in the snow.
quote: a song, about a lost child travelling in the snow, from Tiny Tim, who had a plaintive little voice
why: A one-time song performance and voice texture; unlikely to be contradicted.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge is overcome with penitence and grief on hearing the Ghost quote his own words about the surplus population back at him.
quote: Scrooge hung his head to hear his own words quoted by the Spirit, and was overcome with penitence and grief.
why: A momentary emotional reaction, though it motivates change; the reaction itself is a feeling in the moment.

subject: desolate-moor
statement: The moor is bleak and desert, strewn with monstrous masses of rude stone, with water held prisoner by frost and nothing growing but moss, furze and coarse rank grass.
quote: they stood upon a bleak and desert moor, where monstrous masses of rude stone were cast about, as though it were the burial-place of giants
why: Set dressing of the landscape in a one-off visit; unlikely to be called back.

subject: desolate-moor
statement: The sun sets in the west as the Ghost and Scrooge arrive on the moor, and night falls fully while they are there.
quote: Down in the west the setting sun had left a streak of fiery red
why: Sunset and darkness is momentary atmosphere; time of day is vague and not a lasting anchor.

subject: miners-hut
statement: The miners' hut has walls of mud and stone, which Scrooge and the Spirit pass through to enter.
quote: Passing through the wall of mud and stone, they found a cheerful company assembled round a glowing fire.
why: Wall material and passing through it is incidental texture of the moment.

subject: lighthouse
statement: The lighthouse has thick stone walls with a loophole through which the keepers' firelight shows onto the sea.
quote: through the loophole in the thick stone wall shed out a ray of brightness on the awful sea
why: Loophole and firelight is set dressing of the lighthouse, unlikely to be returned to.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge remains unaltered in outward form during the night while the Ghost grows older.
quote: while Scrooge remained unaltered in his outward form, the Ghost grew older, clearly older
why: Scrooge's unchanged outward form is a general observation; the Ghost's aging is covered elsewhere and nothing depends on this.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: By this point Scrooge is well used to ghostly company, having already been visited by several spirits, yet he fears the silent Phantom more than any spectre he has seen.
quote: "I fear you more than any spectre I have seen.
why: His fear of the Phantom is a feeling in the moment, and the 'well used to ghosts' remark is an aside.

subject: london-exchange-business-district
statement: The merchants gather on 'Change, where they hurry up and down, chink money in their pockets, converse in groups, consult their watches and toy with great gold seals.
quote: on 'Change, amongst the merchants; who hurried up and down, and chinked the money in their pockets, and conversed in groups, and looked at their watches, and trifled thoughtfully with their great gold seals
why: Generic sensory texture of the Exchange crowd's behavior in the moment; nothing later depends on it.

subject: old-joes-rag-and-bone-shop
statement: The shop door's hinges are rusty and screech, and Joe's parlour is the space behind the screen of rags.
quote: The parlour was the space behind the screen of rags.
why: Door hinges and the parlour layout are set dressing unlikely to matter later, though the shop is revisited only in this scene.

subject: old-joe
statement: Joe paid out the gains from a flannel bag of money, telling the sums out on the ground.
quote: old Joe, producing a flannel bag with money in it, told out their several gains upon the ground
why: How Joe paid out the money is a momentary action detail nothing later depends on.

subject: dead-mans-dark-chamber
statement: A cat is tearing at the door of the death-room and rats gnaw beneath the hearth-stone.
quote: A cat was tearing at the door, and there was a sound of gnawing rats beneath the hearth-stone.
why: The cat and rats are sensory texture of the moment and the story does not depend on them later.

subject: debtor-familys-home
statement: The scene takes place by daylight, with the dinner kept warm by the fire for the husband.
quote: revealed a room by daylight, where a mother and her children were
why: Daylight and the dinner kept by the fire are momentary set dressing, though the time of day is minor.

subject: mrs-cratchit
statement: Mrs. Cratchit's eyes are weak and the colour of the sewing hurts them by candle-light; she hides weak eyes from Bob.
quote: "The colour hurts my eyes," she said.
why: Momentary eye strain from candle-light and sewing colour; incidental to the scene.

subject: mrs-cratchit
statement: Mrs. Cratchit and her daughters are sewing work that will be finished long before Sunday.
quote: They would be done long before Sunday, he said.
why: The sewing work is set dressing; details of the task are unlikely to matter later.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge does not yet know whose death the future visions concern; he asks the Spirit who the dead man was and must learn the name.
quote: Tell me what man that was whom we saw lying dead?
why: Scrooge's ignorance is momentary and resolved within the scene when he reads the name on the stone.

subject: ghost-of-christmas-yet-to-come
statement: During the confrontation the Ghost's hand appears to shake and tremble, and it repulses Scrooge when he catches its hand.
quote: For the first time the hand appeared to shake.
why: The hand's trembling and repulsing him is a momentary gesture within the scene; the Ghost then vanishes into a bedpost.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge's bed-curtains are still hanging, rings and all, and were not torn down.
quote: they are not torn down, rings and all.
why: Bed-curtains hanging is momentary set dressing; later scenes are unlikely to depend on it.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge is dressing himself in day garments and stockings, turning some inside out and putting them on upside down, tearing some and mislaying others.
quote: His hands were busy with his garments all this time; turning them inside out, putting them on upside down, tearing them, mislaying them, making them parties to every kind of extravagance.
why: Fumbling with clothes is a moment-to-moment action and figurative extravagance, with no lasting consequence.

subject: ebenezer-scrooge
statement: Scrooge wrote the turkey's delivery address himself, with an unsteady hand.
quote: The hand in which he wrote the address was not a steady one, but write it he did, somehow
why: The unsteady handwriting is a momentary physical manner; nothing later depends on it, though it reflects excitement.

subject: first-portly-gentleman
statement: The portly gentleman addresses him as "Mr. Scrooge" as a question, uncertain at first that it is the same man.
quote: "Mr. Scrooge?"
why: A momentary reaction of uncertain recognition, a question in the moment, with nothing later depending on it.

subject: bob-cratchit
statement: Bob Cratchit believes Scrooge has gone mad, thinking of knocking him down with the ruler and calling for a strait-waistcoat.
quote: He had a momentary idea of knocking Scrooge down with it, holding him, and calling to the people in the court for help and a strait-waistcoat.
why: Bob's momentary idea of knocking Scrooge down is a passing reaction in the moment, and later events do not depend on it.
